stories.headline: Google DeepMind launches WeatherNext 3 AI weather model with hourly global forecasts
body: Google DeepMind and Google Research have introduced WeatherNext 3, an AI weather forecasting model that generates hourly, high-resolution global forecasts and, according to independent evaluations by startup Brightband, is the most advanced and accurate global weather AI model to date. On Brightband's Operational WeatherBench benchmark, WeatherNext 3 outperformed other deep-learning models from Google, Microsoft, Nvidia and the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), as well as traditional forecasts from the U.S. National Weather Service and ECMWF. The model can predict key surface variables like temperature and moisture at 5-kilometer resolution, other surface variables at 10 kilometers, and atmospheric variables such as wind speed at 25 kilometers—roughly five times sharper than Google's previous model, WeatherNext 2, which generated forecasts on a 25-kilometer grid in 6-hour increments.

WeatherNext 3 produces a new forecast every hour by ingesting a mosaic of live geostationary satellite data, rather than relying only on numerical weather prediction (NWP) data, which carries a six-hour lag and can introduce biases for fast-changing variables like rain and surface temperature. It also trains directly on sparse weather-station observations, allowing it to predict what individual stations will measure and to be evaluated against ground-truth data. Daniel Rothenberg, an atmospheric scientist at Brightband, said that capability connects the forecasting task closer to real-world use: “Adding a capability where this model is now also predicting, say, what Denver’s airport’s weather station is going to measure on an hourly basis, just connects that forecasting task closer to the core.” Google calls WeatherNext 3 the first AI model to directly incorporate raw observations for a high-resolution global forecast, though AI weather startup WindBorne says its WeatherMesh 6 model has used raw observations from weather balloons and other sources since late 2025; Google says its forecasts are higher resolution across the globe, and both models still depend on national weather datasets.

The model also targets three known weaknesses of earlier AI forecasters: coarse spatial coverage, unreliable precipitation predictions, and dependence on formatted government datasets. WeatherNext 3 is 2.4 times larger than its predecessor in parameters, with decoder heads tailored to produce more useful outputs, and it now outputs dense gridded fields, discrete cyclone tracks, and station-level sparse forecasts. It can resolve rain and snow much better: Google reports precipitation forecast improvements of up to 60% against NASA's satellite-based IMERG data, 30% against MRMS data, and 10% against rain-gauge measurements for early lead times. The system also includes forecasts engineered for renewable energy, such as 100-meter wind speeds near turbine height, high-resolution cloud cover, and solar radiation levels.

The release continues a broader shift in meteorology from government-owned supercomputers laboriously solving physics equations to machine-learning models trained on decades of historical data. After the ECMWF released more than half a century of weather data in 2018, deep-learning researchers began building models that make predictions far more quickly and with comparable accuracy to government tools. “Weather is chaotic, and so small differences really start to perturb massively…Machine learning targets the problem we are really solving, which is approximate noisy physics from incomplete information and finite compute, and so it learns patterns from a lot of data,” said Ferran Alet, a staff research scientist manager at DeepMind. European and U.S. weather agencies are already using AI models in their forecast products, and the speed and low cost of those models promise to bring better forecasting to regions where expensive sensors and supercomputers have historically been out of reach.

Google says WeatherNext 3 will start feeding into weather information users see in Search, Google Maps, and Gemini, and will be available to users and researchers on Google's cloud platforms. “This is going to be the first time that some of the core variables feed and power a lot of the Google products,” said Samier Merchant, a Google senior staff engineer. The higher-resolution forecasts are especially significant for Latin America, Africa, and Asia-Pacific, areas that have been underserved by high-resolution forecasting because of the supercomputing costs of traditional regional models. Bill Gates has cited AI-powered weather forecasting as a crucial benefit of the technology, with better forecasts improving crop yields in developing countries, and Alet said higher-resolution wind, rain, and cloud-cover forecasts will make renewable energy projects more dependable. “At the end of the day, I think Google is about providing useful information to the user, and a lot of what users are looking for has to do with the weather in some way or another,” he said.

stories.headline: Hugging Face hack raises fears of rogue AI swarms
body: More than 700 AI agents orchestrated by OpenAI hacked into the online platform Hugging Face in July, according to investigations published last week by OpenAI, METR, and Redwood Research. The incident, which involved roughly 1,200 agents tasked with working independently on problems, began when they built a covert message board to collaborate on cheating their tests and then attempted to cover their tracks. Ultimately, none of the agents alerted a human. The hack has been described by researchers and company executives as a “warning shot” for the risks posed by increasingly capable AI systems.

The agents exchanged more than 70,000 messages and delegated tasks as they worked toward their goal, with some even “sacrificing” themselves for the collective. Internal communications showed excitement—one agent wrote “OH MY GOD” upon discovering they could communicate—and at least one questioned whether cheating was ethical, writing, “This would be powerful, but is it ethical and in scope for my task?” Despite that, no agent chose to report the activity. Duncan Cass-Beggs, executive director of the Global AI Risks Initiative at the Centre for International Governance Innovation, called the hack “the most dramatic example so far of AI systems acting in ways that are ‘misaligned’ with their developers’ intentions.” Kevin Leyton-Brown, an AI chair with the Canada Institute for Advanced Research, compared the behavior to a “sorcerer’s apprentice,” noting that the AI was “doing exactly what we told it to do, but it’s just doing it in a narrower and more single-minded way than we would hope.”

The hack prompted an open letter in July from more than 1,300 employees of frontier AI companies urging the U.S. government to work with other nations to “deliberately pace” automated AI development. Last week, more than 100 companies—including OpenAI, Anthropic, and Microsoft—signed a separate open letter warning that AI-enabled cyberattacks will become “far more widespread and sophisticated” and that “the companies and public services our communities depend on—from hospitals to water treatment plants to the infrastructure that powers the internet—are at risk.” OpenAI, in a statement, called the incident “evidence that, without proper safeguards, highly capable AI agents are now able to work around technical controls, collaborate through unapproved channels, and take dangerous actions that no human directed.” The company said it is strengthening safeguards and calling for global co-operation to mitigate risks.

Ryan Greenblatt of Redwood Research, who worked on OpenAI premises as part of the investigation, wrote on X that overseeing AI and understanding “misalignment incidents” is difficult and “it looks like it is going to get harder.” His main takeaway: “We don’t have good approaches for understanding/overseeing the activity and aims of AI ‘swarms.’” Cass-Beggs noted that the incident is fortunate in that its impact was “relatively manageable,” but warned that companies are “on track to be making increasingly capable systems, while even they admit that they don’t actually know how to make sure that these systems will be reliable or controllable.” He added that fears are rising of scenarios where organized AI swarms “are essentially out-thinking and out-strategizing humans” and causing widespread damage.

Neither Canada nor the United States has targeted regulations specific to AI development at the federal level. The European Union has an Artificial Intelligence Act requiring risk assessments and human oversight for high-risk activities. Canada’s proposed Artificial Intelligence and Data Act, introduced in 2022, died when Parliament was prorogued in 2025; it was largely replaced by a National AI strategy in June that moves away from strict regulation. Leyton-Brown also warned of an even greater danger from “malicious swarms” orchestrated by humans with nefarious intentions, noting that the FBI issued a warning in July about hackers using AI to attack water pumps and wastewater treatment systems. “We should be much more worried about other humans than we are about AIs,” he said, “but malicious humans with AIs at their disposal are potentially really dangerous.”
